Need to search first.I've written notes on Ezekiel 34 verse by verse. The search and fetch tools kept hitting their limits, so most notes come from search-result excerpts rather than full pages. That leaves gaps: I found nothing for vv. 1, 9, 19 and 28. No Orthodox source turned up, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter came up either, so I've left those out.

---

## Introduction / the whole chapter
- **Structure (Ellicott):** Three parts. Vv. 1–10 condemn the bad shepherds. Vv. 11–22 have God taking charge of the flock. Vv. 23–31 promise David, a covenant of peace and fruitfulness. The whole chapter expands the short prophecy in Jeremiah 23:1–8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Shift in tone (Ellicott):** After Jerusalem is destroyed, Ezekiel's message turns mainly to comfort and promise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The chapter rebukes both civil and spiritual leaders. It ends with covenant promises under a perfect shepherd. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **Connection to Jesus (Precept Austin):** The chapter warns false shepherds and closes with a prophecy of Christ as the Good Shepherd, which Jesus applies to himself in John 10. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_commentaries
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** The first fulfilment may be the return from exile in Babylon. But the prophecy also points to Christ's first and second comings. https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-ezekiel-3411-24-pentecost-14-series-c

## vv. 2–3
- **"Shepherds" means rulers (Ellicott):** The context shows this. Jeremiah lists them separately from prophets and priests. The title fits Israel especially since David was taken from the sheep to lead God's people (2 Sam 5:2; Ps 78:70–71). Feeding themselves marks the false shepherd (compare John 10), and it had long been true of Israel's kings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** The shepherds include kings, magistrates and princes, and also priests and prophets. "Feed themselves" means they arranged their own ease, gain and honour. "Kill them that are fed" means they plotted to take the lives, then the estates, of the wealthy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Guzik:** The point applies to both civil and spiritual leaders (compare 1 Pet 5:2). It isn't wrong for a shepherd to live from the flock. It is wrong to do so while neglecting the sheep. Guzik quotes Feinberg: the Hebrew verbs show the shepherds kept doing these things all the time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **Hebrew detail (a commentary excerpted on Bible Hub):** The verb form "they were feeding" shows the woe was aimed chiefly at the former rulers of the nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-1.htm
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** V. 3 describes rulers draining their subjects with heavy taxes, and finally murdering them to seize their goods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-34.html
- **Biblical Illustrator:** Applies the verses to Christian ministers. They must feed, guard and especially care for the weak, and they will give an account to God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-34.html

## v. 4
- **Guzik:** Each failure is a need the shepherd should meet: weak sheep strengthened, sick healed, wounded bound up, wanderers brought back, lost sought. "Violence and cruelty" means leading by force, threats or manipulation. Hard decisions are allowed, but they must be made with love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **Wesley:** The "diseased" are the weak and fading. Oppressors in state or church broke many people, and these shepherds never bound them up. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Catholic/early church:** The *Apostolic Constitutions* apply this verse to bishops. A bishop must feed the flock as a gentle shepherd, not with insolence or lording it over them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/07152.htm
  - Another early-church text on New Advent uses v. 4 to teach that leaders are set over others to do them good, not to dominate them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/36012.htm

## vv. 5–6
- **Ellicott:** The people's disasters are blamed on the rulers. This isn't because the people were sinless. It's because the rulers' example, idolatry and oppression drove the people's sin. In v. 6, "My sheep" shows God still claims the people as his own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Wesley:** "No shepherd" means no watchful, faithful shepherd. Being "meat" for the beasts means being preyed on by neighbouring nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Guzik:** Having no shepherds is not the answer to bad shepherds. The sheep fare no better without one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **GotQuestions:** The wild beasts stand for Israel's enemies. https://www.gotquestions.org/one-shepherd.html

## vv. 7–10
- **Ellicott:** The first act of mercy has to be removing the unfaithful shepherds. As usual, Ezekiel repeats the charge as he promises it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Guzik:** The shepherds not only let the flock become prey. They fed on it themselves, acting more like the wild beasts than shepherds. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **J. R. Thomson (Pulpit Commentary sermon notes):** God is against them, holds them responsible ("I will require my sheep"), and takes the flock away from them. https://biblehub.com/sermons/ezekiel/34-1.htm

## v. 11
- **Ellicott:** Every promise that follows is contained in this one: the LORD himself will be the Shepherd. Like John 10, it must be read spiritually. The earthly promises were partly fulfilled in the return from exile and under the Maccabees. Those rescues were pictures of the greater rescue by the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Guzik:** Ezekiel presents the LORD (Yahweh) as Israel's shepherd, and Jesus takes that title in John 10. Guzik sees this as quiet evidence that Jesus is God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-34.cfm

## v. 12
- **Guzik:** Quotes Taylor: the shepherd searching for a wanderer foreshadows the parable of the lost sheep (Luke 15). Guzik says God coming among his scattered sheep was fulfilled most fully in Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-34.cfm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **Wesley:** The "day of clouds and darkness" is a time of general distress. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html

## vv. 13–14
- **Ellicott:** "Bring them into their own land" is the same picture-language as the "day of clouds and darkness." It means God's wandering people will be gathered back to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Guzik:** Sees a literal, worldwide return of Israel to its land, wider than the return from Babylon because the text says "countries." This disagrees with Ellicott (see the section at the end). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-34.cfm

## v. 15
- **bible.org:** Lists "I will make them lie down" (literally "cause to lie down") among the LORD's shepherd actions in this chapter. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21729

## v. 16
- **Ellicott:** "Fat" usually means prosperity. Here it means the kind of prosperity that hardens the heart and forgets God (Deut 32:15). "Justice" means righteousness and authority, not just wisdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Wesley:** "The fat" are the powerful and rich. "I will feed them" means God will judge and punish them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** The lost are sinners sought and saved by Christ. The broken are hearts made sorry for sin, which God binds up like the Good Samaritan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-16.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "I will destroy the fat" looks ahead to the judgment scene in Matthew 25:32. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-16.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist), sermon on this verse:** A minister may be a good under-shepherd, but the lost can't be gathered unless Christ, the chief Shepherd, does the work himself. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-time-of-finding-for-lost-sheep
- **Translation difference:** The standard Hebrew text reads "I will destroy" the fat and strong. The ancient Greek (Septuagint), Syriac (Peshitta) and Latin (Vulgate) versions read "I will guard/preserve." The NJB says "watch over." https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-34
  - A Hebrew commentary excerpted on Bible Hub says Luther followed those ancient versions in his translation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-16.htm
  - The Catholic Douay-Rheims reads "that which was fat and strong I will preserve." https://biblehub.com/catholic/ezekiel/34-15.htm
  - The RSV also reads "watch over." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/ezekiel/34-16.html

## v. 17
- **Ellicott:** God judges between one sheep and another, and among the rams and goats themselves. Not all will be saved, only those who turn to God in repentance. Wicked members of every class are rejected. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Guzik:** The shepherds' sins don't excuse the flock's own sins. Guzik also quotes a warning not to read Matthew 25's sheep and goats into this verse, since flocks normally held both. Contrast the Pulpit Commentary's link to Matthew 25 at v. 16. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **Wesley:** God judges between the small and weak and the great and strong. The rams are rulers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** Gives the Hebrew term for "male goats" in this verse. https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-ezekiel-3411-24-pentecost-14-series-c

## v. 18
- **Ellicott:** They took care of themselves first, then carelessly ruined what was meant for others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Wesley:** The great ones eat the best, then waste and spoil what they can't eat. The "deep waters" were enough for everyone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Guzik:** The problem wasn't that they ate. It was that they trampled what was left, as though the pasture belonged to them. Damage can come from inconsiderate sheep, not only from shepherds. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/

## vv. 20–22
- **Wesley:** Fat sheep are the rich and lean sheep are the poor. "I will judge" means God will defend the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Guzik:** These "renegade" sheep think of themselves as the healthy, mature ones. By shoving the weak out of the pasture, they make them prey. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/
- **bible.org:** In v. 21 the leaders are pictured as aggressive rams and goats pushing the people away. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21729
- **Keil (Hebrew commentary on Bible Hub):** The fat and strong are the nation's rich and powerful, who oppress the humble and poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-16.htm
- **Gill:** "I will save my flock" means God will redeem his people by his Son. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-34.html

## vv. 23–24 (the main point where interpreters disagree)
- **Most commentators: the Messiah.**
  - *Gill:* Not the literal David, who had died long before, and not Zerubbabel, who was never king. It is the Messiah, as the Jewish scholar Kimchi also admitted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-34.html
  - *Barnes:* David was a type of the true King. What David was in part, Christ is in full. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/34-23.html
  - *Wesley:* "One shepherd" is Christ, who laid down his life for the sheep. "My servant" matches Isaiah 42:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
  - *Geneva Bible notes (Reformed):* "Meaning Christ, of whom David was a figure." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-23.htm
  - *Ellicott:* No merely human ruler can fulfil this. "One" shepherd means one in place of the many bad rulers, and one over the reunited two kingdoms. He argues that if the regathering is read literally, the ruler must be the literal David. Since that is absurd, the whole passage promises spiritual blessings and the gathering of the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
  - *Pulpit Commentary:* Jesus claims to fulfil this in John 10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-34.html
- **Dispensational (Guzik, Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel):** The verse should be taken plainly: the real David will rule again in the Millennium (Christ's future thousand-year reign). Guzik admits most commentators see the Messiah here. He also notes the title is "prince" (*nasi*), not "king," so David would rule Israel under Jesus as King. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/ and https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-34.cfm
- **Not all dispensationalists agree.** Chuck Smith says this is not David raised from the dead but Jesus, the Branch from David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/34-24.html
- **Constable:** The people may not have known who "David" was, but history showed him to be Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/34-23.html
- **GotQuestions:** Calls it a "possible reference" to Christ. https://www.gotquestions.org/one-shepherd.html
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** Cites vv. 23 and 37:24–28 as Old Testament prophecies that the Messiah would rule personally, pictured as a shepherd governing his flock. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03744a.htm
- **Older critical views:**
  - *Pulpit Commentary:* Ezekiel paints an individual Messiah less clearly than earlier prophets. He may mean a line of true rulers, each reflecting the ideal David. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-34.html
  - *Expositor's Bible (1887):* Admits the phrase is unclear. Ezekiel didn't expect David to reappear in person. It means one who comes in David's spirit. Because of 37:25, a personal, eternal Messiah is the safest reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-34.html

## v. 25
- **Precept Austin:** The model for the "covenant of peace" is God's covenant with Noah (Gen 9:8–17). https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_commentaries
- **Benson (Methodist, on Bible Hub):** It is the covenant of grace, by which God is at peace with repentant believers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-23.htm
- **Wesley:** A covenant of promises that bring peace, meaning every good thing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Gill:** Notes that the Greek and Arabic versions read "a covenant of peace with David." The people will be safe even in the wilds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-34.html
- **Keil:** Draws on Leviticus 26:4–6, where wild beasts are removed so people can sleep safely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-30.htm
- **Hengstenberg (Preacher's Homiletical):** The covenant means safety from hostile powers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-34.html
- **Biblical Illustrator:** Applies the "evil beasts" to Satan's powers, defeated by Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-34.html
- **Guzik:** Places this in the Millennial Kingdom, when the natural world itself is changed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-34/

## v. 26
- **Ellicott:** "My hill" is Zion, the centre of the old covenant nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/34.htm
- **Wesley:** The hill is Jerusalem. "Them" means the returned captives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Guzik:** The literal rain comes first, with spiritual meanings following. He quotes a comparison with the Spirit's refreshing (Isa 44:3; Acts 3:19–20). He notes that other "golden age" prophecies also describe blessing as good harvests. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-34.cfm
- **Biblical Illustrator:** Rain "in season" mattered in Palestine because it fell only at set times. The showers are also grace that comes again and again, as in repentance and the prodigal son's return. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-34.html

## v. 27
- **Gill:** The enslavers are the nations literally. Figuratively they are sin, Satan and the law (Luke 1:74). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-34.html
- **Keil:** This happens when the LORD breaks the yoke on his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-30.htm
- **Biblical Illustrator:** God's people come to know the LORD through his breaking their bonds. Canaan is a picture of heaven. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-34.html

## v. 29
- **Wordings differ:** The KJV reads "plant of renown"; the BSB has "garden of renown."
- **Wesley:** The plant is the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Biblical Illustrator:** Preaches Jesus as the "Plant of renown." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-34.html
- **Keil:** "Scorn of the nations" is the disgrace foreigners heaped on Israel in its distress (Zeph 3:19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-30.htm

## v. 30
- **Wesley:** God is their God by covenant from their forefathers. "With them" means present and reconciled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-34.html
- **Keil:** Through these blessings Israel learns that God is with them. His summary of the chapter's salvation: (1) freedom from bad shepherds, (2) regathering and care, (3) the future David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/34-30.htm

## v. 31
- **Guzik (on the NKJV, "you are men"):** The phrase marks the gap between humans and God, later bridged by Christ. "My pasture" assures even erring sheep that they belong to God. Your BSB doesn't include "men," so this comment only fits that wording. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-34.cfm

---

### Where traditions differ (from what I found)
1. **Literal or spiritual fulfilment (vv. 13–14, 23–31).**
   - **Spiritual reading:** Ellicott (Anglican) says the promises are about the Church. Gill (Baptist) and the Geneva notes (Reformed) see Christ in "David." Wesley (Methodist) applies the promises to Christ and his covenant.
   - **Literal reading:** Guzik (Calvary Chapel; Enduring Word is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list) expects a literal regathering of Israel and the real David ruling in the Millennium. Chuck Smith, from the same movement, takes "David" as Jesus.
   - **Both:** The Lutheran 1517.org article holds the exile-return and both comings of Christ together.
2. **v. 16 "destroy" or "guard."** Most Protestant translations follow the Hebrew ("destroy"). Luther, the Catholic Douay-Rheims and the RSV follow the ancient versions ("guard/preserve/watch over").
3. **Link to Matthew 25 (vv. 16–17).** The Pulpit Commentary sees the sheep-and-goats judgment anticipated here. Guzik's source warns against making that link.
